title: Stiffness vs. Strength: Definitions & Comparisons for Better Performing Parts
summary: Compare stiffness vs. strength, including Young’s modulus, yield strength, and tensile strength, and see how each property affects part performance.
body_markdown:
Stiffness and strength both describe how a material responds to an applied load, but they measure different


behaviors. Stiffness is a material’s resistance to elastic deformation, while strength describes how much stress it can withstand before yielding or failing. A material can be strong without being particularly stiff, or stiff without having exceptionally high strength.


That distinction matters when material properties translate into the performance of a manufactured part. A


component that needs to


maintain its shape under load presents a different material requirement from one that needs to withstand a high load without permanent deformation or failure.


Several mechanical properties help quantify these


behaviors. Young’s modulus, also known as the modulus of elasticity, is commonly used to compare material stiffness. Strength can be described using properties such as yield strength and ultimate tensile strength, depending on the material and how the part will be loaded.


---


---


## What is Material Stiffness?


Stiffness describes a material’s resistance to elastic deformation under load. In practical terms, a stiffer material will deflect less than a less stiff material subjected to the same stress.


As long as the material


remains within its elastic region, it returns to its original shape when the load is removed.


Material stiffness is commonly quantified using


Young’s modulus


, or the modulus of elasticity. A higher Young’s modulus


indicates a stiffer material. Steel, for example, has a much higher Young’s modulus than


aluminum, so a steel specimen will experience less elastic strain when subjected to the same tensile stress.


Young’s modulus is a material property, but the stiffness of a finished part also depends on its geometry. Increasing the thickness or changing the cross-section of a


component can significantly reduce deflection without changing materials. This distinction is useful when comparing material data: Young’s modulus describes the material itself, while part stiffness describes how the complete


component responds to a load.


---


## What Is Material Strength?


Strength describes a material’s ability to withstand stress without permanent deformation or failure. Unlike stiffness, there


isn’t a single value that defines how strong a material is. The relevant measurement depends on the type of loading and the point at which performance is considered unacceptable.


Yield strength


identifies the stress at which a material begins to deform permanently.


Ultimate tensile strength (UTS)


is the maximum tensile stress it can withstand before failure begins. Other measurements, including compressive, shear, and flexural strength, characterize performance under different loading conditions.


This is why greater strength


doesn’t automatically mean greater stiffness. A material may tolerate high stresses before yielding while still deforming


considerably within its elastic range. Conversely, a highly stiff material may resist deflection well but fail at a lower stress. Comparing the


appropriate mechanical property to the demands of the part gives a more useful picture of expected performance.


---


## What’s the Difference Between Stiffness and Strength?


The simplest distinction is that


stiffness


determines how much a material deforms under load, while strength


determines how much stress it can withstand before permanent deformation or failure


.


Consider a bracket supporting a load. If it bends enough to interfere with another


component but returns to its original shape afterward, stiffness is the limiting factor. If the load causes the bracket to remain bent, it has exceeded its yield strength. Increase the load further and it may eventually reach its ultimate strength and fail.


The stress-strain curve helps illustrate the relationship. Young’s modulus is calculated from the slope of the elastic


portion of the curve, where deformation is reversible. Yield strength marks the transition into permanent, or plastic, deformation. Ultimate tensile strength occurs later, at the maximum engineering stress reached during a tensile test.


These properties answer different questions, so a higher value for one does not imply a higher value for the other.

---


## How Do Stiffness and Strength Compare Across Materials?


The difference becomes clearer when comparing material families. Metals


generally have much higher Young’s modulus values than unfilled thermoplastics, which means they typically deform less under equivalent stress. Within metals, however, strength can vary


substantially even when stiffness


remains


relatively similar.


Steel is a good example. Different steel grades and heat treatments can produce


large differences in yield and tensile strength, while their Young’s modulus values


remain comparatively close. This means switching to a higher-strength steel does not necessarily make a part significantly stiffer.


Aluminum illustrates the distinction from another angle. Its Young’s modulus is


roughly one-third that of steel, so equivalent geometries will


generally deflect more under the same loading conditions. Its lower density, however, can make it useful where stiffness


relative to weight matters, and geometry can be adjusted to increase part stiffness.


Polymers add another layer. Their mechanical


behavior can be more sensitive to temperature, moisture, loading rate, and reinforcement. Adding glass


fiber to a thermoplastic, for example, can


substantially increase its modulus as well as affect its strength. For manufactured plastic parts, the specific grade and associated material data are therefore more informative than comparisons based on polymer family alone.


---


---


## How Stiffness and Strength Affect Part Performance


The geometry of a


component


determines how


material properties translate into its response to a load.


Part stiffness can often be increased through geometry without changing the material. Increasing a section’s thickness, adding ribs, or changing its cross-sectional shape can reduce deflection by increasing its resistance to bending. This is why two parts made from the same material can behave very differently under identical loads.


Strength is also affected by geometry, particularly where features create localized stress concentrations. Sharp internal corners, holes, notches, and abrupt changes in cross-section can increase local stresses and create potential failure points. Fillets and smoother transitions can help distribute those stresses more evenly.


When it comes to comparing manufacturing processes: an injection-molded


fiber-reinforced plastic may have direction-dependent properties because of


fiber orientation and material flow. With


[3D printing](https://www.protolabs.com/services/3d-printing/) , mechanical properties can vary with build orientation and process.


[CNC machining](https://www.protolabs.com/services/cnc-machining/) starts with established stock material properties, but geometry still


determines how effectively a finished part resists deformation and failure.


Ultimately, stiffness and strength answer different questions about how a part will perform. One


determines how readily it deforms; the other, how much stress it can withstand. Looking at both in the context of part geometry, operating conditions, and manufacturing process provides a more complete picture of material performance and helps


identify where design or material changes will have the greatest effect.


---


## FAQ


---


### Can a material have high strength but low stiffness?


*expand_less* *expand_more*


Yes. Strength and stiffness are independent properties, so a material can withstand


relatively high stress before yielding while still experiencing significant elastic deformation. Some polymers


provide a useful example, combining high strength with


considerably lower stiffness than metals. This is why strength alone cannot predict how much a part will deflect under load.


### Does increasing part thickness increase strength or stiffness?


*expand_less* *expand_more*


Increasing thickness can improve both, but its effect on stiffness can be particularly significant in bending. A thicker cross-section has a greater moment of inertia, which reduces deflection without changing the material’s Young’s modulus. Added thickness can also reduce stress within a part, although the effect depends on its geometry and loading conditions.


### Why is it that two materials with similar tensile strength perform differently Under load?


*expand_less* *expand_more*


Tensile strength describes only one aspect of material


behavior. Two materials with similar tensile strength can have different Young’s modulus, yield strength, ductility, and fatigue characteristics, causing them to respond differently to the same load. Part geometry and operating conditions also influence performance, so similar tensile strength values do not necessarily


indicate comparable


behavior in a finished


component.
